1:
What kind of vain is meant divides them. Ellicott says the English draws too much attention to the result: it should be not vain rather than not in vain, meaning not purposeless and idle. Robertson supports that from the vocabulary, distinguishing the word here, which means hollow, from another meaning fruitless, and noting that Paul uses both of the same subject elsewhere, since one easily leads to the other — though he allows the pastoral sense too, that every minister watches wistfully to see what will come of his work. Calvin takes it of character in the same way, glossing it by the ambitious man who makes much show and has nothing solid. Henry reports both readings without choosing, that the preaching was not fruitless, as our translation has it, or else that it was not empty and treacherous.

The appeal to Philippi is handled as evidence. Barnes explains where the shame lay — the treatment was wholly undeserved and contrary to the laws — and draws a rule from Paul's willingness to name it: it is not wrong to call things by their right names, and a man who has been abused need not smooth the matter over by pretending otherwise. Robertson adds, after Milligan, that more than the bodily suffering it was the indignity offered to a Roman citizen that stung, and that the memory still rankled — an instance, he says, of Acts and the epistles throwing light on each other. Ellicott quotes Bengel that this was enough to have scared others, and notes the marks of the ill usage were still fresh when they reached Thessalonica; such men, he adds, were not likely to be empty. Clarke presses the word for conflict, which means not only intense labour but exposure to the greatest danger, and quotes the Greek saying that in danger one must not delay.

The three disclaimers are then sorted. Calvin assigns each to a department: the first to the substance of the doctrine, the second to the affections of the heart, the third to the manner of acting — so that Paul denies in turn that they were deluded, that they came under any impure desire, and that they used fraud. Ellicott raises a question about the first word, whether it means deceit or simply error. If error, he says, the argument would be that of Paley's Evidences, deducing the truth of a revelation from the sufferings of those who bring it — but the contrasts drawn in the following verses seem to preclude that sense. Robertson takes the passive sense of error anyway, and derives the word for guile from a verb meaning to catch with bait.

On uncleanness the readings diverge widely, and the divergence is about where the danger lies. Clarke and Robertson locate it outside: Clarke in the Gentile philosophers and their gods, celebrated for adulteries and thefts and barbarities, and Robertson in a remark of Lightfoot's that the disclaimer, startling as it seems, was not needless amid the impurities consecrated by the religions of the day, since the popular mind saw no necessary connection between religion and morals and the ecstatic initiations were grossly sensual. Ellicott turns it inward instead: the word may mean only impure or covetous motives, but it probably refers to the subtle forms of temptation that often accompany spiritual work. Wesley notes only that the term is not always confined to lust. Gill and Clarke agree that the word rendered exhortation carries consolation as well, the gospel consisting of doctrines full of comfort, so that every word of such preaching was consolatory. Henry closes the matter where the chapter opens it, that it is a great comfort to a minister when his own conscience and the consciences of others witness together that he set out well.
4:
The word rendered allowed is really a word of testing. Ellicott points out that it implies examination and approval, that it recurs a few words later rendered trieth, and that the tense should be have been rather than was, since Paul argues from habitual practice: examined and approved by God, they study to please the God who keeps examining them rather than court those they are sent to. Robertson reads the perfect the same way, and calls the following clause a confident claim of loyalty which ought to be every preacher's ambition. Calvin guards it from the other side, that Paul does not boast of being approved as though he were such of himself, nor set his own power against the grace of God; Gill says the same, that no previous worthiness was in them. Barnes draws a rule: a deep conviction of the truth of religion restrains a man from trick, since artifice is the usual accompaniment of a bad cause.

What counts as flattery is answered doctrinally by one and rhetorically by the rest. Gill lists what they refused to flatter with: not the purity of human nature but original sin and the corruption of all its powers, not free will but man's impotency, and a plain warning that they would perish unless they repented. Barnes keeps to manner rather than matter — no praising of beauty, wealth or talent while concealing painful truths — and calls flattery the deceiver's principal art. Robertson notes that an Epicurean wrote a treatise on flattery, and that Milligan finds here a rebuke to the rhetoricians of the day. Calvin puts the logic tightly: a man set on pleasing men must stoop to flattery, and a man intent on duty will keep at a distance from any appearance of it.

On covetousness the striking thing is that two commentators independently notice how Paul chooses his witnesses. Wesley observes that for the flattering words he appeals to the Thessalonians, that being an open fact, and for the cloak of covetousness to God, that being a secret of the heart — and where the matter is mixed, to both. Ellicott makes the same distinction independently. Barnes and Calvin agree that the word for cloak means a show put forward to cover a real intent, Calvin adding that it works like a trap, as men spread nets for birds. Robertson remarks that the sin of wanting more is especially fatal in a preacher. Clarke turns from exposition to attack, addressing the clergy of his own church: can you call God to witness that your ministry has no end but his glory in the salvation of souls, or did you enter the priesthood for a morsel of bread, for what is ominously and impiously called a living? In better days, he says, the office was called a cure of souls — what care have you for the souls of those whose labours more than support you?

The last clause turns on one word. Calvin denies it refers to money: the connection requires the sense of dignity, since Paul is saying he waived even his just claim to authority and refrained from every show of preeminence, as though he had been a minister of the common rank. Ellicott agrees, preferring the margin — to have dealt heavily with them in all the pomp of apostolic dignity — and holds that more is meant than obtaining the maintenance an apostle might claim. Barnes reports both senses undecided. Clarke settles it by the Hebrew, whose word answering to this Greek one signifies weight and glory alike, and says the apostle uses it in both; Robertson reports Milligan's view that Paul plays on the double sense. Ellicott adds that the title of apostle is extended to Silas and Timothy as it is to Barnabas in Acts, and suggests that the episcopal office may be ranked with the apostolate.
7:
A single letter divides the commentators here, and the division runs against the usual lines. The manuscripts are split between a word meaning gentle and a word meaning babes. Robertson prefers babes on the documentary evidence, noting that four named scholars prefer the other because it makes better sense, that one calls the reading impossible, and that this is too strong, since Paul is fond of the word — Lightfoot admitting only that he works the metaphor to the limit in his passion. Clarke rejects it on the sense: it can never be original, since the scope of the place is wholly against it, the Thessalonians being the children and the apostles the nurse, and a man cannot say he was among them as a little child while professing to be their nurse. Calvin reports the variant, notes that the older translation and Wicliff read little, and declines to choose, since either way the point is a voluntary abasement. Gill observes that one word becomes the other by adding a letter, and both come to much the same.

The nurse herself is examined closely. Robertson and Ellicott both press the possessive, Robertson identifying the word as the mother-nurse who suckles her own and finding the usage in Sophocles. Ellicott sets the picture against its background — the fawning, greedy, vainglorious teachers Greeks were accustomed to, against apostles sitting like mothers among their own children and folding them to their bosoms — and quotes a modern Frenchman for the rule that made his life winning, to keep a mother's heart for men. Calvin describes the affection as rare and wonderful, a woman who spares no labour, shuns no anxiety, is wearied by no assiduity and cheerfully gives her own blood to be sucked. Henry notes the gentleness came from one who might have used an apostle's authority, and is the way to win people rather than rule with rigour, a nursing mother bearing with frowardness and stooping to mean offices for the child's good. Wesley changes the figure to a hen surrounded by her young.

Imparting their own souls is then weighed against imparting the gospel. Ellicott keeps the metaphor running: the gospel was the milk given to young converts, but these nurses were ready to let them draw their very life away. Barnes builds a scale — to tell a man the way of salvation is itself a proof of love, as it is love to tell one in danger of a way of escape, but a much higher love to tell a lost sinner how he may be saved. Robertson traces the rare verb for longing after them, which is known chiefly from a Lycaonian gravestone where sorrowing parents greatly desire their son, and calls it a term of endearment from the language of the nursery.

The manual labour raises a question about a right waived. Chrysostom lays down that a teacher ought to do nothing with a feeling of burden which tends to his disciples' salvation, and that if Jacob was buffeted night and day keeping flocks, much more should the man entrusted with souls endure toil however mean; he then sets Paul's practice against the ordinance that those who preach should live of the gospel — but I, says Paul, would not. Calvin makes it law: the churches are bound to maintain their ministers, so Paul did more than his office required, and avoided burdening not only the church but any individual, moved by some special consideration, since elsewhere he used his liberty freely. Clarke infers a chronology from the wording, that Paul stayed at Thessalonica much longer than is generally supposed, and pictures him working by day and preaching at night; Barnes reverses it, having him preach by day and make up the labour at night. Ellicott separates the two words for toil, the first naming the kind of work and the second its intensity.
10:
Ellicott justifies the double appeal from philosophy: God is called because the readers could judge only the outward propriety of their teachers, and it is a moral law, as Aristotle says, that the righteous man is not he who does acts righteous in themselves but he who does them in the mind that befits righteous men. The three adverbs are divided, and each divides them differently: Wesley among God, men and ourselves; Clarke among God, men and the minister's own conduct; Ellicott into two, the inner life and the outer; Robertson insisting there is a reason for each. Calvin makes the third a matter of reputation and explains the qualifying clause: the servants of Christ cannot escape calumny, since being hated by the world they must be evil spoken of among the wicked, so the claim is restricted to those who judge uprightly. Ellicott reads that same clause in the opposite direction, as naming the place where, if anywhere, they might have been tempted to be lax or exorbitant.

Barnes marks its limits: it is no claim to absolute perfection but to consistency of character and faithfulness in duty, which every Christian should be able to make. Clarke marvels at it — what consciousness of integrity a man must have, since no hypocrite could appeal at once to God and to his hearers. Robertson infers a considerable stay at Thessalonica, longer than the three sabbaths Luke records, and adds that a pastor ought to live so that his life will bear inspection.

What follows is taken as evidence of method. Ellicott finds in the words about every one a glimpse of the apostolic practice of dealing with individual souls, and quotes an earlier expositor's exclamation that not one in all that multitude was passed over; Clarke says none was left unnoticed or uncomforted. Calvin makes it a standard for the office: no one will be a good pastor who does not show himself a father to his church, and it is not enough to teach all in common from the pulpit without particular instruction as need requires, as Paul admonished both publicly and from house to house. On the three participles Wesley is briefest: by exhorting we are moved to do a thing willingly, by comforting joyfully, by charging carefully. Robertson calls them three phases of a minister's preaching. Barnes presses the third, properly testified: they came as witnesses from God and did not teach the gospel's duties as their own; Ellicott would render it adjured.

The last verse turns on a tense. Ellicott says the true reading is not that God has called but that he was calling, altered to avoid a slight theological difficulty — the call being no momentary act but a continual beckoning until the privileges offered are attained. Robertson confirms the participle keeps on calling. On the kingdom and the glory Clarke divides them, the church here being the kingdom among men and the glory hereafter, but allows the phrase may be a hendiadys for his glorious kingdom; Wesley divides them the same way in six words; Robertson takes the kingdom as the future consummation because of the glory attached, though Paul uses the word of the present kingdom of grace too. Barnes explains walking worthy by the child who honours a parent, keeping his commands and carrying the family principles into his life. Gill guards the imitation, that we copy not God's perfections, which are inimitable, nor his power and wisdom, but his kindness and beneficence and righteousness. Calvin ends on the manner of preaching: it is lively when men are not merely told what is right but pricked by exhortation and summoned to the judgment-seat of God, lest they sleep in their vices — and if men so prompt needed stirring, what must be done with us, in whom the sluggishness of the flesh reigns more?
13:
Ellicott finds two different verbs where the English has one: the first an outward receiving, the second the welcome given — so that Paul is thankful less for the manner in which the word was greeted than for what it essentially was. Robertson remarks that Paul had no doubt he was proclaiming God's message; should a preacher preach his doubts, if he has any? Henry sets out three consequences: that the gospel comes by men of like passions, the treasure being in earthen vessels; that it is nevertheless God's word in truth; and that those are greatly to blame who give out their own fancies for it. Barnes makes the ground of conviction decisive for endurance: a man convinced by human reasoning may have his faith shaken by opposite reasoning, one won by eloquence will not be proof against the same arts used for error, and one who embraces religion out of respect for a pastor or parent has nothing that will abide a fiery trial. Calvin argues from the other end, that once the persuasion has taken hold obedience follows of necessity, since who would not shudder at resisting God — so that the contempt in which many hold scripture is itself evidence of what they take it to be.

Being imitators of the Judean churches is then put to three quite different uses. Barnes reads it pastorally: the likeness is in suffering, not constitution, and persecution by those claiming to be God's people is no evidence against a church being true. Clarke reads it polemically: the honour of being a model belonged to Judea and not to Rome, which had no such preeminence, or the apostle would have proposed it. Robertson reads it critically, quoting Lightfoot that this affectionate admiration of the Jewish churches is entirely subversive of the theory of a feud between Paul and the Twelve. Gill notes that the Syriac renders the word became like them and the Arabic equal to them, the equality lying in persecution. Ellicott suggests the Judean churches were chosen as the oldest and best organised and the most afflicted, and notes that persecuting through others was the standing policy, which shows the Thessalonian church was almost wholly Gentile.

The invective that follows is the hardest thing in the chapter, and they handle it with differing restraint. Clarke draws up a numbered indictment of six counts and presses each to its limit, ending that they persecuted the body to death and the soul to damnation. Calvin says the apostle strips them of all honour, but asks the question that qualifies it — why the same persons are said to have killed both the prophets and Christ — and answers that it refers to the entire body, there being nothing new in their resisting God. Barnes enters a qualification of his own on the clause about not pleasing God, that it does not mean they were not aiming to please him. Wesley narrows the charge of being contrary to all men, resting it chiefly on the attempt to hinder others from hearing the gospel. Two commentators supply the check the passage most needs. Ellicott observes that the memories of Stephen's speech seem to be waking in a man who had himself once been a persecuting Jew, and Robertson says it outright: those who thought they pleased God by such work were doing what Paul did when he ravaged the young church at Jerusalem, and Paul knows better now. Ellicott also puts the passage to critical use: since a Hebrew of the Hebrews could write of the Jews so in an undisputed letter, the objection that no born Jew could have written so in the fourth Gospel falls. Calvin names the difficulty underneath: these converts were harried by the one nation that gloried in the name of God, and might well ask what that implied about the religion they had just embraced.
16:
Barnes states the charge precisely, narrowing it. The Jews did not hold it unlawful to speak to Gentiles, nor even to offer them eternal life; they held that any who were saved must be saved as Jews, born such or made such by proselytism. Paul maintained the opposite, that a heathen might be saved without circumcision — and that, not Gentile evangelism as such, was the point at issue. Gill adds that even believing Jews at first disapproved of the word being carried to the nations. Calvin explains why the apostle presses it at such length: they exclaimed everywhere that Paul profaned the gospel by publishing it among the Gentiles, and by that calumny divided churches, took from the Gentiles the hope of salvation and obstructed the gospel — so the passage removes a stumbling-block rather than gratifies indignation. Robertson notes the same hostility was being shown at Corinth as Paul wrote.

Ellicott reads the filling up of sin carefully. It is not their intention in forbidding, he says, but the end to which such conduct tends; and he draws the principle wide — there may be a sum of wickedness God allows a nation, a church or a person to complete before cutting them off from spiritual help. He corrects the conjunction, which is not for but but, so that they were working up to the rounded perfection of their sin when the wrath came upon them first; and notes that the verb is the one used of a sudden apparition, and should be the simple past. Robertson leaves open whether it is God's plan or the natural result of continual sinning; Wesley says only that vengeance overtook them unawares while they sought to destroy others.

The word rendered taken from you means bereaved, and the closer readers press it. Barnes says it describes the condition of an orphan, so that no word could express a stronger attachment; Clarke complains that we tamely translate a word meaning bereft of children; Ellicott calls it a return to the earlier figure of the mother; Robertson tracks the sequence, from nurse to babe to father and now to orphan, four figures in one chapter. Calvin quotes a description of the grief with which dying parents leave children helpless. On the phrase for the time of an hour, Robertson observes that it had seemed long to Paul, and Ellicott that so far were they from the proverb about being out of mind when out of sight that absence increased the yearning. Henry turns it on the reader: our time on earth is short whether we are with our friends or absent from them, and this world is not a place where we are long together, since it is in heaven that holy souls meet and never part. Wesley draws another distinction, that the passage shows not the transient affections of grief or joy, which every reader notices flowing like a torrent in Paul, but the abiding tenderness from which those flow, which requires a nicer attention to discern.

On the hindrance the commentators differ about how far to look. Barnes says the manner is unknown and conjecture useless, but that it is not improper to trace the great enemy's hand in obstacles to duty. Clarke allows either the devil or one of his children, and adds that Paul's friends thought it imprudent to let him go till the storm abated. Wesley identifies the agent as the persecuting Jews. Calvin holds both, that when the wicked molest us they fight under Satan's banner as his instruments, and wishes it deeply impressed on all pious minds that the adversary is continually contriving to obstruct the building of the church. Ellicott takes the singular pronoun as evidence: the words even I show Silas and Timothy did not share the intention, agreeing minutely with the movements in Acts, where both were left behind at Berœa.
19:
Gill begins by saying what the words do not mean. The Thessalonians were the apostle's hope, but not its foundation, which was Christ, nor the thing hoped for, which was eternal life, nor its ground, which was the blood and righteousness of Christ — they were persons of whom he hoped well, and steadfastly. Calvin enters the same guard on the crown: it is not that Paul glories in anyone but God, but that we are allowed to glory in all God's favours in their own place, provided he remains the object of aim. From this he concludes that Christ's ministers will share in glory according as each has promoted his kingdom, and should learn now to rejoice in nothing but the prosperous issue of their labours.

The figure behind the crown is disputed. Barnes takes the allusion to be to the victors at the Grecian games, and Ellicott agrees, calling it a crown one is proud to wear and paraphrasing the thought as the pride of presenting them to Christ. Robertson proposes another occasion: a king or conqueror arriving on a visit was given a chaplet of glorying, and the word used here for the coming is almost technical in the papyri for the arrival of a ruler expecting his crown of coming — so the crown belongs to a royal entry rather than a footrace. He adds that Paul is answering an insinuation that he did not really wish to come at all. Clarke puts the argument as a question: having forsaken everything for the gospel and having no prospects from earth, why should he labour at the risk of his life except to get their souls saved?

Both Barnes and Clarke close the chapter by turning it into an examination for ministers, and their conclusions are worth setting side by side. Clarke says every man who preaches should examine himself by this chapter, and that most doing so conscientiously will either give their place up or resolve to work more fervently; those who enter for applause or emolument may have their reward, but one smile of approbation from Christ is not included in it. He adds that God often permits the most benevolent purposes of his servants to be frustrated for a time. Barnes shuts two doors at once. A minister should not make it his point to please men — but if he does please them, and his ministry is acceptable, he should not take that as proof of unfaithfulness, since he ought to have a good report of them that are without; and neither should he aim to displease them, or count the offence he gives as evidence that he is faithful. He ends on the friends already gone: of many of the living it is true that the best and dearest they have are already in heaven, and how should their hearts pant to meet them there.

The last word of the chapter belongs to Clarke, and it sits oddly against the invective he had drawn up four verses earlier in six numbered counts. Having said there that the persecutors hated the whole human race, he closes by writing that we cannot pretend to say for what end God has preserved the Jews distinct from all the peoples among whom they sojourn, but that it must unquestionably be for an object of the very highest importance — and that in the meantime the Christian world should treat them with humanity and mercy. Wesley adds only that they are his crown as well as his other children are, and Gill that they were the seals of his ministry and would be his joy for ever.
